subject: Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?

messages.author: 7f87f78f0cd24437
messages.subject: Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?
parts:
Hello Everyone,

 

I have a slightly complicated situation, and I would appreciate people’s thoughts on the appropriate way to proceed. Apologies for the long background description.

 

I have multi-species bird point count data collected in a range of habitat types, including continuous forest and open farmland. Unsurprisingly, detectability varies between habitat type. (I checked this by comparing pooled CDS and MCDS with habitat as a covariate, and AIC always selects the MCDS models).

 

In some cases the habitat patches were so large that I could be certain that the intervening habitat was uniform. However, in others (particularly the farmland) there are lots of small patches of different habitat (e.g. fields, forest fragments etc.) So just because I was counting in a field, doesn’t mean that I couldn’t detect a bird singing in a forest patch 200m away. And in that situation, I could detect that species at a much greater distance than I could have if it had just been uniform forest between me and the bird.

 

Point count locations were assigned randomly, so birds’ distributions should not be influenced by them directly. However, birds were distributed non-randomly with respect to habitat, as species are often habitat-specific (i.e. the forest-adapted birds are only going to be in the forest patches and not in the fields). I can’t lump the detections of those forest birds in farmland together with detections of the same species from the continuous forest because the calls will have attenuated in different ways between the habitats. However, I sense that it would also be wrong ignore the habitat differences, and treat all of the farmland detections as if they came from a uniform habitat.

 

Therefore, would it be better to only include those species that I detected in the same habitat in which I was counting? (i.e. only include birds detected in fields when I was standing in fields, and discarding those detected in forest patches). Alternatively, I may be over-thinking this. The dataset is fairly large (~10,000 detections per habitat), and there are many point counts, in multiple landscapes with different configurations. So perhaps the effect of the patchy landscape will even out across the whole dataset.

 

In addition, should I run stratified analyses for each habitat type, or am I able to stick with the MCDS model with habitat as a covariate, and just produce abundance estimates in that way?

 

I would be interested to hear others’ opinions about my reasoning and intended approach.

 

Thanks in advance,

Tom

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?
parts:
Tom, yes, I think you are over-thinking it.  If your aim is just to estimate abundance (or density), then you can just analyse data from all points together.  You can use MCDS and use for example an open-ness covariate, but even if you ignore the big differences in detectability between points and use CDS, pooling robustness means that you get very little bias in your estimates.  (You can try it both ways to verify this.)  By pooling the data, you will need to choose a truncation distance that’s satisfactory in woodland, so you will end up truncating a lot of your detections in open habitat.

 

Pooling robustness doesn’t apply if you need to estimate density separately by habitat type, so mcds is better for that.  As you note, classifying habitat type is problematic, because of its patchy nature.  You can stratify your area by habitat type, and for points in one habitat from which you detect birds in a second habitat, you can include those detections when analysing densities in that second habitat.  The discussion in the 2004 adv ds book on buffer zones is relevant here.  But it gets a bit messy.

 

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 7f87f78f0cd24437
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?
parts:
Dear Steve,

Thank you for your prompt response. I do need to estimate density per habitat type, so I will proceed with MCDS. Please can you clarify, when you say "for points in one habitat from which you detect birds in a second habitat, you can include those detections when analysing densities in that second habitat." Are you suggesting that I can combine detections of forest birds in farmland together with detections of the same species from the continuous forest and analyse them together? My sense was that the calls will have attenuated in different ways between the habitats, and so it wouldn't be legitimate to combine them. Or, are you saying that I should estimate species densities separately (i.e. for forest patches in farmland, and for continuous forest), and then calculate a mean density for the two types of forest in combination?

Kind regards,
Tom

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?
parts:
There is no single right way to do this.  What you can do is define habitat strata, and divide your survey region into strata.  It is up to you whether you combine small patches of woodland with continuous forest.  My comment was simply to indicate that you can include detections made in a given habitat from a point in another habitat in your analysis for the first habitat.  This issue is discussed on pp192-194 of the 2004 adv ds book.

 

Steve
